subject: Consolidating GitHub + CircleCI + Snyk into GitLab for platform reliability
body:
Hi GitLab team,

I'm the CTO at Guild Education, a Colorado-based education benefits platform. We've grown fast and the toolchain grew with us. Today we're running source on GitHub, CI on CircleCI plus a scattering of Jenkins jobs, artifacts split across registries, and security coverage spread between Snyk, ad hoc container scans, and homegrown checks. It works, but not cleanly. We spend too much time stitching signals together during incidents and audits.

Two drivers are pushing us toward consolidation. First: reliability. Our devs lose hours each week to brittle pipeline dependencies and inconsistent runners across teams. Second: governance. We're operating under SOC 2 expectations and customer questionnaires are getting sharper on SDLC controls, audit trails, and secret handling.

We're evaluating a move to GitLab to reduce the surface area: one platform for SCM, CI/CD, security scanning, approvals, and audit history. What I need is a clear path for a phased migration — repo migration first, then pipelines, then security controls — without forcing a big bang cutover.

Scope: ~450-600 dev seats, plus build users. Budget range is $250K-$450K ACV depending on security bundles and support. If you can show how GitLab replaces our current mix with better visibility, we'll move quickly into a 30-60 day pilot.

Thanks,
Donnie Flood
CTO, Guild Education

subject: GitHub Enterprise migration + pipeline standardization (need proposal in March)
body:
Hi GitLab,

Luke Swanson, CTO at Ibotta (NYSE: IBTA). We're a Denver-based performance marketing platform serving 200 million consumers. We're heavy on mobile + backend services, and pipeline throughput matters because release velocity directly affects retailer campaigns.

Our current setup is GitHub Enterprise for source control, Jenkins for most CI, and growing dependency on paid CI add-ons. Security is layered but uneven: some repos have SAST gates, others rely on code review discipline, and container scanning varies by team. When something breaks, we diagnose across GitHub, Jenkins, and a separate vulnerability tool.

We're considering GitLab as a single platform for SCM + CI/CD + DevSecOps. Biggest questions: 1) Runner strategy at scale on Kubernetes. 2) Enforceable SAST/DAST/dependency scanning with exceptions and audit trails. 3) Migration mechanics for hundreds of repos without disrupting delivery.

We'd run a pilot with ~75 engineers across 10-15 services, then expand. If the pilot looks good, $600K-$900K ACV depending on seat count and support. Can you connect us with someone who can show a real migration playbook? If we get a proposal in March, we can pilot in April.

Regards,
Luke Swanson
CTO, Ibotta

subject: Evaluating GitLab Self-Managed for regulated SDLC controls and platform consolidation
body:
Hello,

Bernard Harguindeguy, SVP & CTO at Ping Identity. We're a Denver-based identity and access management provider with ~2,200 employees post-merger with ForgeRock. Our customers expect mature SDLC controls, traceable changes, and a strong security posture.

We've handled that historically with best-of-breed tools: separate SCM, CI, scanning, approvals, and ticketing. The problem is proving everything consistently across products, especially when auditors and enterprise customers ask for end-to-end evidence.

We're exploring GitLab Self-Managed as a consolidation move. Requirements: tight SSO/SCIM integration with fine-grained access controls, expansive audit logs, core DevSecOps scanning standardized across product teams, and flexible deployment for multi-cloud workloads.

We're not ready to rip and replace — GitLab becomes the standard for new services first, then legacy migrates incrementally. This is a material purchase: 1,500-2,500 seats over time, likely $1M+ ACV depending on tier, security, and support.

Best,
Bernard Harguindeguy
SVP & CTO, Ping Identity

subject: Standardizing DevSecOps across business units — need GitLab rollout approach
body:
Hi GitLab team,

I oversee platform engineering for Trimble, a Colorado-based industrial technology company delivering software across construction, geospatial, and connected device ecosystems. Our challenge is scale and fragmentation. Different business units historically chose their own stack: a mix of Git repos, CI systems, artifact tooling, and security scanners. The result is duplicated cost, inconsistent controls, and developer experience that varies wildly.

We're targeting a platform standard in 2026. Requirements: large monorepos and many microservices, hybrid build needs including firmware, policy and governance for enterprise customers, and visibility into supply chain risk including SBOMs and remediation workflows.

GitLab is on our shortlist because the consolidated approach is appealing, but we need confidence it handles organizational change. The operating model matters more than the technical part: how teams adopt, how exceptions are managed, how we produce audit-ready evidence.

We're planning an RFP and a controlled rollout starting with two product lines. Potential scope is several thousand seats with a multi-year commitment. $2M+ ACV is on the table, but only if you demonstrate repeatable rollout patterns and measurable outcomes.

Thank you,
Morgan Chen
VP, Software Platforms, Trimble

subject: Replacing CircleCI + Snyk with GitLab Ultimate for SOC2/PCI evidence
body:
Hi GitLab,

I lead infrastructure engineering at Recurly, a Denver subscription billing company. We've got real compliance expectations — SOC 2 is table stakes, PCI comes up constantly in customer reviews. Our dev teams ship quickly, but our current SDLC tooling is too spread out.

Right now source lives in GitHub and CI is mostly CircleCI. Security scanning is split: dependency checks in one place, container scanning in another, ad hoc scripts for secrets. Every customer security questionnaire means gathering evidence across systems: merge approvals, pipeline logs, vulnerability remediation, change history.

We're researching GitLab to consolidate repos, pipelines, and security controls in a single platform with consistent audit trails. Interested in practical policy model, integrated scanning workflows, and a migration path that won't disrupt delivery. 250-400 developer seats, probably $100K-$250K ACV depending on tier.

Best,
Sam Patel
Head of Infrastructure Engineering, Recurly

subject: Jenkins sprawl and audit pressure — interested in GitLab CI/CD + security
body:
Hello GitLab team,

I run engineering for Vertafore, an insurance software provider in the Denver area. We operate across multiple product lines and a mix of legacy and modern services. Our biggest pain is running and governing delivery at scale.

We've accumulated hundreds of Jenkins pipelines. The plugin ecosystem is a constant source of breakage, and we're carrying tribal knowledge risk. Security expectations have tightened — customers want stronger evidence of SDLC controls and vulnerability management.

We're looking at GitLab CI/CD as a standardized build and deployment backbone with integrated DevSecOps scanning. Business case: replace brittle Jenkins with pipelines-as-code, standardize security scanning policies, and reduce time to produce audit evidence.

We'll run a structured pilot: 5-8 services, migrate pipelines, measure cycle time and failure rate. 800-1,200 potential users. $400K-$800K ACV opportunity depending on roadmap.

Regards,
Dana Ruiz
VP Engineering, Vertafore

subject: Toolchain consolidation: SCM + CI + security gates under one roof
body:
Hi,

I'm the CISO at Conga, a Colorado-based revenue lifecycle software company. We build CLM and related systems, which makes our own SDLC posture visible to customers and prospects. We've layered security controls on a fragmented toolchain — separate systems for repos, builds, artifacts, and scanning. Proving consistent enforcement is a recurring problem.

Current friction: pipelines split across Jenkins and a hosted CI service, artifact provenance spread across tools, SBOM conversations becoming routine with larger customers, and security exceptions handled differently by each team.

I'd like a demo focused on security and compliance controls, audit logging, and policy management across many projects. We're in active evaluation this quarter. If the platform meets requirements, we'll sponsor a POC in 30-45 days. Potential ACV $500K-$1M over time.

Thanks,
Chris Nguyen
CISO, Conga

subject: Enterprise platform consolidation for SDLC — requesting GitLab roadmap + pricing
body:
GitLab team,

Our software environment is broad: internal systems, customer-facing platforms, and partner integrations across multiple regions. Our SDLC toolchain mirrors that scale: multiple SCM solutions, multiple CI engines, mixed artifact repositories, and differing security approaches by team.

Regards,
Taylor Brooks
SVP Technology Platforms, Arrow Electronics

subject: Reducing CI spend and security tool sprawl — looking at GitLab as single platform
body:

Currently on GitHub for source control. CI/CD is a mix of legacy Jenkins plus a hosted provider. Security scanning is split across separate tools. GitLab is attractive because it's one vendor and one workflow. We need: lower total platform cost, faster pipelines with fewer flaky failures, and consistent security posture without drowning devs in false positives. 700-1,200 developer seats over time. ACV could land in $500K-$1M range.

Thanks,
Riley Kim
VP Engineering, Platform, Angi

subject: We sell security outcomes — want GitLab to harden our own SDLC posture
body:
Hello GitLab,

I'm the CTO at Coalfire, a Denver-based cybersecurity and compliance firm. We help clients with assurance programs and secure system delivery. That means our own internal engineering practices are constantly under a microscope. Customers ask how we build, how we scan, and how we prove controls.

We're looking at GitLab to strengthen and standardize our SDLC security controls end-to-end: merge approvals and branch protection, embedded SAST/dependency/container/secrets scanning, centralized audit logging, and vulnerability remediation workflows.

We'd especially like to see how GitLab moves us from compliance as reporting to compliance as controls. I need enforced policy, traceable exceptions, and repeatable evidence.

We'd start with internal product engineering, then expand. 300-600 users. ACV $150K-$300K.

Best,
Jamie Ortiz
CTO, Coalfire

subject: Supply chain security push — need integrated scanning and SBOM discipline
body:

Focus areas: reducing security as an afterthought, managing false positives with policy tiers, clear vulnerability remediation workflows, and credible SBOM generation.

Thanks,
Avery Singh
Head of Engineering, FullContact

subject: Integrating security gates into CI without slowing releases — GitLab evaluation
body:

Regards,
Casey Park
Director, DevSecOps, Webroot

subject: Secure SDLC platform for isolated environments — GitLab Self-Managed discussion
body:

subject: HIPAA-driven DevSecOps controls — need SDLC evidence and security gates
body:

body:
